where (a)(a) follows from Jensen’s inequality, (b)(b) comes from Lem. C.1, and (c)(c) results from the fact that 𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐮‖2]=d\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]=d for 𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}).

Moreover, since the gradient estimator ∇^​F​(𝜽)\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}) is constructed from KK dependent random directions, we have the variance bound:

𝔼​[‖∇^​F​(𝜽)−∇Fμ​(𝜽)‖2]​=(a)​𝔼​[‖∇^​F​(𝜽)‖2]−‖∇Fμ​(𝜽)‖2​≤(b)​𝔼​[‖1K−1​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−Fμ​(𝜽)μ​𝐮k‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\norm{\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}})-\nabla F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}^{2}\right]\overset{(a)}{=}\mathbb{E}\quantity[\norm{\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}})}^{2}]-\norm{\nabla F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}^{2}\overset{(b)}{\leq}\mathbb{E}\quantity[\norm{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}{\mu}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2}] (24)
≤(c)\displaystyle\overset{(c)}{\leq} K(K−1)2​μ2​𝔼​[|f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮‖2]​≤(d)​K​d​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+1))(K−1)2​μ2,\displaystyle\frac{K}{(K-1)^{2}\mu^{2}}\mathbb{E}\quantity[\left|f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]\overset{(d)}{\leq}\frac{Kd\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+1))}{(K-1)^{2}\mu^{2}}\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from (22), (b)(b) comes from getting rid of ‖Fμ​(𝜽)‖2\norm{F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}^{2}, (c)(c) follows from the dependence of random directions {𝐮k}k=1K\{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}, and (d)(d) results from the following inequality:

𝔼​[|f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮‖2]​=(a)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\quantity[\left|f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]\overset{(a)}{=} 𝔼​[|f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)|2​‖𝐮‖2]+𝔼​[|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\quantity[\left|f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]+\mathbb{E}\quantity[\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}] (25)
≤(b)\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{\leq} σξ2​𝔼​[‖𝐮‖2]+𝔼​[|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle\sigma_{\xi}^{2}\mathbb{E}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]+\mathbb{E}\quantity[\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]
≤(c)\displaystyle\overset{(c)}{\leq} σξ2​d+𝔼​[2​(|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−F​(𝜽)|2+2​|F​(𝜽)−𝔼𝐮′​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮′)]|2)​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle\sigma_{\xi}^{2}d+\mathbb{E}\quantity[2\quantity(\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}+2\left|F({\bm{\theta}})-\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}}\quantity[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime})]\right|^{2})\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]
≤(d)\displaystyle\overset{(d)}{\leq} σξ2​d+𝔼​[2​(|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−F​(𝜽)|2+2​𝔼𝐮′​[|F​(𝜽)−F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮′)|2])​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle\sigma_{\xi}^{2}d+\mathbb{E}\quantity[2\quantity(\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}+2\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}}\quantity[\left|F({\bm{\theta}})-F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime})\right|^{2}])\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]
≤(e)\displaystyle\overset{(e)}{\leq} σξ2​d+2​L02​μ2​𝔼​[(‖𝐮‖2+𝔼𝐮′​[‖𝐮′‖2])​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle\sigma_{\xi}^{2}d+2L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}\mathbb{E}\quantity[\quantity(\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}}\quantity[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}}^{2}])\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]
=(f)\displaystyle\overset{(f)}{=} σξ2​d+2​L02​μ2​𝔼​[(‖𝐮‖2+d)​‖𝐮‖2]​=(g)​d​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+1)),\displaystyle\sigma_{\xi}^{2}d+2L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}\mathbb{E}\quantity[\quantity(\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}+d)\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]\overset{(g)}{=}d\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+1))\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from (1), (b)(b) comes from Assump. 4.4, (c)(c) results from the fact that (a+b)2≤2​(a2+b2)(a+b)^{2}\leq 2(a^{2}+b^{2}), (d)(d) follows from Jensen’s inequality, (e)(e) comes from Lem. C.1, and (c)(c), (f)(f), (g)(g) results from the fact that 𝔼​[‖𝐮‖2]=d\mathbb{E}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]=d and 𝔼​[‖𝐮‖4]=d​(d+2)\mathbb{E}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{4}]=d(d+2) for 𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}).

Overall, combining the bias between the smoothed gradient and the true gradient with the variance of the gradient estimator, we have:

𝔼​[‖∇^​F​(𝜽)−∇F​(𝜽)‖2]​≤(a)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\norm{\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}})-\nabla F({\bm{\theta}})}^{2}\right]\overset{(a)}{\leq} 𝔼​[‖∇^​F​(𝜽)−Fμ​(𝜽)‖2]+‖Fμ​(𝜽)−∇F​(𝜽)‖2≤K​d​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+1))(K−1)2​μ2+L12​μ2​d,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\norm{\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}})-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}^{2}\right]+\norm{F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})-\nabla F({\bm{\theta}})}^{2}\leq\frac{Kd\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+1))}{(K-1)^{2}\mu^{2}}+L_{1}^{2}\mu^{2}d\ , (26)

where (a)(a) follows from (22). ∎

The following lemma bounds the bias between the smoothed Hessian and the true Hessian:

Lemma C.3 (Bias of Smoothed Hessian).

Let smoothed objective Fμ​(𝛉)F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}) be (7), we have:

‖∇2Fμ​(𝜽)−∇2F​(𝜽)‖F2≤L22​μ2​d.\norm{\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})-\nabla^{2}F({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}^{2}\leq L_{2}^{2}\mu^{2}d\ . (27)
Proof.
‖∇2Fμ​(𝜽)−∇2F​(𝜽)‖F2​≤(a)​𝔼𝐮​[‖∇2F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−∇2F​(𝜽)‖F2]​≤(b)​L22​μ2​𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐮‖2]​=(c)​L22​μ2​d,\norm{\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})-\nabla^{2}F({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}^{2}\overset{(a)}{\leq}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\norm{\nabla^{2}F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-\nabla^{2}F({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}^{2}\right]\overset{(b)}{\leq}L_{2}^{2}\mu^{2}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right]\overset{(c)}{=}L_{2}^{2}\mu^{2}d\ , (28)

where (a)(a) follows from Jensen’s inequality, (b)(b) comes from Lem. C.1, and (c)(c) results from the fact that 𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐮‖2]=d\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]=d for 𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}). ∎

Lemma C.4 (Bound on Second Moment of ν\nu).

Let ν=(f​(𝛉+μ​𝐮;ξ)−Fμ​(𝛉))/μ2\nu=\quantity(f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}))/\mu^{2}, where 𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}). Under Assump. 4.3 and Lem. C.1, we have:

𝔼​[ν2​‖𝐮‖2]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\nu^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]\leq dμ4​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+1)),\displaystyle\frac{d}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+1))\ , (29)
𝔼​[ν2​‖𝐮‖4]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\nu^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{4}]\leq d​(d+2)μ4​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+2)),\displaystyle\frac{d(d+2)}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+2))\ ,
𝔼​[ν2​‖𝐮‖6]≤\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\nu^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{6}]\leq d​(d+2)​(d+4)μ4​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+3)).\displaystyle\frac{d(d+2)(d+4)}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+3))\ .
Proof.

First,

𝔼𝐮​[ν2​‖𝐮‖2]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\nu^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]= 1μ4​𝔼𝐮​[|f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\left|f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right] (30)
=(a)\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=} 1μ4​𝔼𝐮​[(|f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)|2+|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2)​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\quantity(\left|f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})\right|^{2}+\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2})\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right]
≤(b)\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{\leq} 1μ4​(σξ2​𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐮‖2]+𝔼𝐮​[|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮‖2])\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right])
=(c)\displaystyle\overset{(c)}{=} 1μ4​(σξ2​d+𝔼𝐮​[|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮‖2]),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}d+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right])\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from (1), i.e. 𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)]=0\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})]=0, (b)(b) comes from Assump. 4.4, and (c)(c) results from the fact that 𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐮‖2]=d\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]=d for 𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}).

Furthermore, the second term in (30) can be bounded as:

𝔼𝐮​[|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮‖2]​≤(a)\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right]\overset{(a)}{\leq} 2​𝔼𝐮​[(|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−F​(𝜽)|2+|F​(𝜽)−𝔼𝐮′​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮′)]|2)​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle 2\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\quantity(\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}+\left|F({\bm{\theta}})-\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}}\quantity[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime})]\right|^{2})\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right] (31)
≤(b)\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{\leq} 2​𝔼𝐮​[(|F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−F​(𝜽)|2+𝔼𝐮′​[|F​(𝜽)−F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮′)|2])​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle 2\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\quantity(\left|F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-F({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}}\quantity[\left|F({\bm{\theta}})-F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime})\right|^{2}])\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right]
≤(c)\displaystyle\overset{(c)}{\leq} 2​L02​μ2​𝔼𝐮​[(‖𝐮‖2+𝔼𝐮′​[‖𝐮′‖2])​‖𝐮‖2]\displaystyle 2L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\quantity(\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}}\quantity[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}}^{2}])\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right]
=(d)\displaystyle\overset{(d)}{=} 2​L02​μ2​𝔼𝐮​[(‖𝐮‖2+d)​‖𝐮‖2]​=(e)​4​L02​μ2​d​(d+1),\displaystyle 2L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\quantity(\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}+d)\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}\right]\overset{(e)}{=}4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+1)\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from the fact that (a+b)2≤2​(a2+b2)(a+b)^{2}\leq 2(a^{2}+b^{2}), (b)(b) comes from Jensen’s inequality, (c)(c) results from Lem. C.1, and (d)(d), (e)(e) results from the fact that 𝔼​[‖𝐮‖2]=d\mathbb{E}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]=d and 𝔼​[‖𝐮‖4]=d​(d+2)\mathbb{E}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{4}]=d(d+2) for 𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}).

Overall, substituting (31) into (30), we complete the proof:

𝔼𝐮​[ν2​‖𝐮‖2]≤1μ4​(σξ2​d+4​L02​μ2​d​(d+1))=dμ4​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+1)).\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\nu^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]\leq\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}d+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+1))=\frac{d}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+1))\ . (32)

Similarly, we have:

𝔼𝐮​[ν2​‖𝐮‖4]≤d​(d+2)μ4​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+2)).\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\nu^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{4}]\leq\frac{d(d+2)}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+2))\ . (33)
𝔼𝐮​[ν2​‖𝐮‖6]≤d​(d+2)​(d+4)μ4​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+3)).\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\nu^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{6}]\leq\frac{d(d+2)(d+4)}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+3))\ . (34)

∎

Below are some useful lemmas for N>1N>1 case, which can be proved similarly as above.

Lemma C.5 (Bias of Gradient Estimator (35) for N>1N>1).

Let smoothed objective Fμ​(𝛉)F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}) be (7), and the gradient estimator ∇^​F​(𝛉)\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}) be

∇^​F​(𝜽t−1)≜1N​K−1​∑n,k=1N,Kf​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n,k;ξ)−bμ​𝐮t−n,k,\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-1})\triangleq\frac{1}{NK-1}\sum_{n,k=1}^{N,K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k};\xi)-b}{\mu}{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k}\ , (35)

where the averaged baseline b≜1N​K​∑n,k=1N,Kf​(𝛉t−n+μ​𝐮t−n,k;ξ)b\triangleq\frac{1}{NK}\sum_{n,k=1}^{N,K}f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k};\xi). We then have:

𝔼​[∇^​F​(𝜽t−1)]=1N​∑n=1N∇Fμ​(𝜽t−n).\mathbb{E}[\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-1})]=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\nabla F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n})\ . (36)
Proof.

The bias of the gradient estimator ∇^​F​(𝜽)\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}) follows from Stein’s identity:

𝔼​[∇^​F​(𝜽t−1)]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-1})]= 𝔼​[1N​K−1​∑n,k=1N,Kf​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n,k;ξ)−1N​K​∑n,k=1N,Kf​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n,k;ξ)μ​𝐮t−n,k]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{NK-1}\sum_{n,k=1}^{N,K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k};\xi)-\frac{1}{NK}\sum_{n,k=1}^{N,K}f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k};\xi)}{\mu}{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k}\right] (37)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼​[1N​K−1​∑n,k=1N,KN​K−1N​K​f​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n,k;ξ)−1N​K​∑n′,k′=1(n′,k′)≠(n,k)N,Kf​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n,k′;ξ)μ​𝐮t−n,k]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{NK-1}\sum_{n,k=1}^{N,K}\frac{\frac{NK-1}{NK}f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k};\xi)-\frac{1}{NK}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n^{\prime},k^{\prime}=1\\ (n^{\prime},k^{\prime})\neq(n,k)\end{subarray}}^{N,K}f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k^{\prime}};\xi)}{\mu}{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k}\right]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼​[1N​K​∑n,k=1N,Kf​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n,k;ξ)μ​𝐮t−n,k]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{NK}\sum_{n,k=1}^{N,K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k};\xi)}{\mu}{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k}\right]
−𝔼​[1N​K​(N​K−1)​∑n,k=1N,K∑n′,k′=1(n′,k′)≠(n,k)N,Kf​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n,k′;ξ)μ​𝐮t−n,k]\displaystyle\quad-\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{NK(NK-1)}\sum_{n,k=1}^{N,K}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}n^{\prime},k^{\prime}=1\\ (n^{\prime},k^{\prime})\neq(n,k)\end{subarray}}^{N,K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k^{\prime}};\xi)}{\mu}{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k}\right]
=(a)\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=} 𝔼𝐮​[1N​∑n=1NF​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n)μ​𝐮t−n]​=(b)​1N​∑n=1N∇Fμ​(𝜽t−n),\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n})}{\mu}{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}\right]\overset{(b)}{=}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\nabla F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n})\ ,

where (a)(a) comes from the dependence of different random directions {𝐮t−n,k}k=1K\{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n,k}\}_{k=1}^{K}, and (b)(b) follows from Stein’s identity.

∎

Lemma C.6 (Bound on Second Moment of ν\nu for N>1N>1).

Let νt−1=(f​(𝛉t−1+μ​𝐮t−1;ξ)−b)/μ2\nu_{t-1}=\quantity(f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-1}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-1};\xi)-b)/\mu^{2}, where bb is the averaged baseline in Thm. 4.7, and 𝐮t−1∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}_{t-1}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}). Under Assump. 4.3 and Lem. C.1, for N>1N>1 case, we have:

∑n=1N𝔼​[νt−n2​‖𝐮t−n‖2]≤\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\quantity[\nu_{t-n}^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}]\leq λ2​N​(N​K−1)2​dλ2​μ4​(N​K−1)2−L02​η2​μ2​K​(N2−1)​d/3​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+1)),\displaystyle\frac{\lambda^{2}N(NK-1)^{2}d}{\lambda^{2}\mu^{4}(NK-1)^{2}-L_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}K(N^{2}-1)d/3}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+1))\ , (38)
∑n=1N𝔼𝐮​[νt−n2​‖𝐮t−n‖4]≤\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\quantity[\nu_{t-n}^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{4}]\leq λ2​N​(N​K−1)2​d​(d+2)λ2​μ4​(N​K−1)2−L02​η2​μ2​K​(N2−1)​d​(d+2)/3​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+2)),\displaystyle\frac{\lambda^{2}N(NK-1)^{2}d(d+2)}{\lambda^{2}\mu^{4}(NK-1)^{2}-L_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}K(N^{2}-1)d(d+2)/3}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+2))\ ,
∑n=1N𝔼𝐮​[νt−n2​‖𝐮t−n‖6]≤\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\quantity[\nu_{t-n}^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{6}]\leq λ2​N​(N​K−1)2​d​(d+2)​(d+4)λ2​μ4​(N​K−1)2−L02​η2​μ2​K​(N2−1)​d​(d+2)​(d+4)/3​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+3)).\displaystyle\frac{\lambda^{2}N(NK-1)^{2}d(d+2)(d+4)}{\lambda^{2}\mu^{4}(NK-1)^{2}-L_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}K(N^{2}-1)d(d+2)(d+4)/3}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+3))\ .
Proof.

First, at the iteration t−nt-n, we have:

𝔼𝐮​[νt−n2​‖𝐮t−n‖2]=\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\quantity[\nu^{2}_{t-n}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}]= 1μ4​𝔼𝐮​[|f​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n;ξ)−1N​∑n′=1NFμ​(𝜽t−n′)|2​‖𝐮t−n‖2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\left|f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n};\xi)-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}\right] (39)
=(a)\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=} 1μ4​𝔼𝐮​[(|f​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n;ξ)−F​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n)|2+|F​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n)−1N​∑n′=1NFμ​(𝜽t−n′)|2)​‖𝐮t−n‖2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\quantity(\left|f({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n};\xi)-F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n})\right|^{2}+\left|F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n})-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}})\right|^{2})\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}\right]
≤(b)\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{\leq} 1μ4​(σξ2​𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐮t−n‖2]+𝔼𝐮​[|F​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n)−1N​∑n′=1NFμ​(𝜽t−n′)|2​‖𝐮t−n‖2])\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}]+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\left|F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n})-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}\right])
=(c)\displaystyle\overset{(c)}{=} 1μ4​(σξ2​d+𝔼𝐮​[|F​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n)−1N​∑n′=1NFμ​(𝜽t−n′)|2​‖𝐮t−n‖2]),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}d+\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\left|F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n})-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}\right])\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from (1), i.e. 𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)]=0\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})]=0, (b)(b) comes from Assump. 4.4, and (c)(c) results from the fact that 𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐮‖2]=d\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{2}]=d for 𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}).

Furthermore, the second term in (39) can be bounded as:

𝔼𝐮​[|F​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n)−1N​∑n′=1NFμ​(𝜽t−n′)|2​‖𝐮t−n‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\left|F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n})-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}\right] (40)
=(a)\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=} 𝔼𝐮​[(|F​(𝜽t−n+μ​𝐮t−n)−Fμ​(𝜽t−n)|2+|Fμ​(𝜽t−n)−1N​∑n′=1NFμ​(𝜽t−n′)|2)​‖𝐮t−n‖2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\quantity(\left|F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n})-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n})\right|^{2}+\left|F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n})-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}})\right|^{2})\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}\right]
≤(b)\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{\leq} 4​L02​μ2​d​(d+1)+|Fμ​(𝜽t−n)−1N​∑n′=1NFμ​(𝜽t−n′)|2⋅𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐮t−n‖2]\displaystyle 4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+1)+\left|F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n})-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}})\right|^{2}\cdot\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}\right]
=\displaystyle= 4​L02​μ2​d​(d+1)+|1N​∑n′=1N(Fμ​(𝜽t−n)−Fμ​(𝜽t−n′))|2⋅d\displaystyle 4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+1)+\left|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}\quantity(F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n})-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}}))\right|^{2}\cdot d
≤(c)\displaystyle\overset{(c)}{\leq} 4​L02​μ2​d​(d+1)+d​L02N​∑n′=1N‖𝜽t−n−𝜽t−n′‖2\displaystyle 4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+1)+\frac{dL_{0}^{2}}{N}\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}\norm{{\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}}}^{2}
≤(d)\displaystyle\overset{(d)}{\leq} 4​L02​μ2​d​(d+1)+d​L02​η2​μ2​K​Cνλ2​N​(N​K−1)2⋅∑n′=1N|n−n′|,\displaystyle 4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+1)+\frac{dL_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}KC_{\nu}}{\lambda^{2}N(NK-1)^{2}}\cdot\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N}|n-n^{\prime}|\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from the fact that 𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)]=Fμ​(𝜽)\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})]=F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}), (b)(b) comes from (31), (c)(c) results from Lem. C.1, and (d)(d) results from:

‖𝜽t−n−𝜽t−n′‖2​≤(a)\displaystyle\norm{{\bm{\theta}}_{t-n}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime}}}^{2}\overset{(a)}{\leq} ∑n′′=min⁡(n,n′)max⁡(n,n′)‖𝜽t−n′′−𝜽t−n′′+1‖2≤η2​∑n′′=min⁡(n,n′)max⁡(n,n′)‖H~−1​(𝜽t−n′′)​∇^​F​(𝜽t−n′′)‖2\displaystyle\sum_{n^{\prime\prime}=\min(n,n^{\prime})}^{\max(n,n^{\prime})}\norm{{\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime\prime}}-{\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime\prime}+1}}^{2}\leq\eta^{2}\sum_{n^{\prime\prime}=\min(n,n^{\prime})}^{\max(n,n^{\prime})}\norm{\widetilde{H}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime\prime}})\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-n^{\prime\prime}})}^{2} (41)
≤(b)\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{\leq} η2​μ2​K​Cνλ2​(N​K−1)2​|n−n′|,\displaystyle\frac{\eta^{2}\mu^{2}KC_{\nu}}{\lambda^{2}(NK-1)^{2}}|n-n^{\prime}|\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from the triangle inequality, and (b)(b) follows from the result in (92), and we define the constant upper bound CνC_{\nu} such that ∑n𝔼​[νt−n2​‖𝐮t−n‖2]≤C\sum_{n}\mathbb{E}\quantity[\nu_{t-n}^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}]\leq C for all nn.

Overall, substituting (40) into (39), and summing over nn, we have:

∑n=1N𝔼𝐮​[νt−n2​‖𝐮t−n‖2]≤\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[\nu_{t-n}^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}]\leq 1μ4​(σξ2​d​N+4​L02​μ2​d​(d+1)​N+d​L02​η2​μ2​K​Cνλ2​N​(N​K−1)2⋅∑n,n′=1N|n−n′|)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}dN+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+1)N+\frac{dL_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}KC_{\nu}}{\lambda^{2}N(NK-1)^{2}}\cdot\sum_{n,n^{\prime}=1}^{N}|n-n^{\prime}|) (42)
=\displaystyle= 1μ4​(σξ2​d​N+4​L02​μ2​d​(d+1)​N+d​L02​η2​μ2​K​Cν​(N2−1)3​λ2​(N​K−1)2).\displaystyle\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}dN+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+1)N+\frac{dL_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}KC_{\nu}(N^{2}-1)}{3\lambda^{2}(NK-1)^{2}})\ .

Note that the definition of CνC_{\nu} implies that:

Cν=1μ4​(σξ2​d​N+4​L02​μ2​d​(d+1)​N+d​L02​η2​μ2​K​Cν​(N2−1)3​λ2​(N​K−1)2),C_{\nu}=\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}dN+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+1)N+\frac{dL_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}KC_{\nu}(N^{2}-1)}{3\lambda^{2}(NK-1)^{2}})\ , (43)
Cν=1μ4​(σξ2​d​(d+2)​N+4​L02​μ2​d​(d+2)2​N+d​(d+2)​L02​η2​μ2​K​Cν​(N2−1)3​λ2​(N​K−1)2),C_{\nu}=\frac{1}{\mu^{4}}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}d(d+2)N+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}d(d+2)^{2}N+\frac{d(d+2)L_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}KC_{\nu}(N^{2}-1)}{3\lambda^{2}(NK-1)^{2}})\ , (44)

which leads to:

∑n=1N𝔼​[νt−n2​‖𝐮t−n‖2]≤λ2​N​(N​K−1)2​dλ2​μ4​(N​K−1)2−L02​η2​μ2​K​(N2−1)​d/3​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+1)).\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}\quantity[\nu_{t-n}^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{2}]\leq\frac{\lambda^{2}N(NK-1)^{2}d}{\lambda^{2}\mu^{4}(NK-1)^{2}-L_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}K(N^{2}-1)d/3}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+1))\ . (45)

Similarly, we have:

∑n=1N𝔼𝐮​[νt−n2​‖𝐮t−n‖4]≤λ2​N​(N​K−1)2​d​(d+2)λ2​μ4​(N​K−1)2−L02​η2​μ2​K​(N2−1)​d​(d+2)/3​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+2)),\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\quantity[\nu_{t-n}^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{4}]\leq\frac{\lambda^{2}N(NK-1)^{2}d(d+2)}{\lambda^{2}\mu^{4}(NK-1)^{2}-L_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}K(N^{2}-1)d(d+2)/3}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+2))\ , (46)
∑n=1N𝔼𝐮​[νt−n2​‖𝐮t−n‖6]≤λ2​N​(N​K−1)2​d​(d+2)​(d+4)λ2​μ4​(N​K−1)2−L02​η2​μ2​K​(N2−1)​d​(d+2)​(d+4)/3​(σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+3)).\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\quantity[\nu_{t-n}^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-n}}^{6}]\leq\frac{\lambda^{2}N(NK-1)^{2}d(d+2)(d+4)}{\lambda^{2}\mu^{4}(NK-1)^{2}-L_{0}^{2}\eta^{2}\mu^{2}K(N^{2}-1)d(d+2)(d+4)/3}\quantity(\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+3))\ . (47)

∎

C.2 Proof of Lem. 3.1

Proof.

We first derive the first derivative of the single-step policy optimization objective (7) by applying the Policy Gradient Thm. (Sutton et al., 1999):

∇Fμ​(𝜽)=𝔼𝐱∼π𝜽​(𝐱)​[∇ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱)​𝔼ξ​[f​(𝐱;ξ)]].\nabla F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}\sim\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\nabla\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\mathbf{x}};\xi)]\right]\ . (48)

Taking the second derivative, we have:

∇2Fμ​(𝜽)=\displaystyle\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})= ∇​∫π𝜽​(𝐱)​∇ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱)​𝔼ξ​[f​(𝐱;ξ)]​𝑑𝐱​=(a)​∫(∇π𝜽​(𝐱)​(∇ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱))⊤+π𝜽​(𝐱)​∇2ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱))​𝔼ξ​[f​(𝐱;ξ)]​𝑑𝐱\displaystyle\nabla\int\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\nabla\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\mathbf{x}};\xi)]d{\mathbf{x}}\overset{(a)}{=}\int\quantity(\nabla\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\quantity(\nabla\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}}))^{\top}+\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\nabla^{2}\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}}))\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\mathbf{x}};\xi)]d{\mathbf{x}} (49)
=(b)\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{=} ∫π𝜽​(𝐱)​((∇ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱))​(∇ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱))⊤+∇2ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱))​𝔼ξ​[f​(𝐱;ξ)]​𝑑𝐱\displaystyle\int\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\quantity(\quantity(\nabla\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}}))\quantity(\nabla\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}}))^{\top}+\nabla^{2}\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}}))\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\mathbf{x}};\xi)]d{\mathbf{x}}
=\displaystyle= 𝔼𝐱∼π𝜽​(𝐱)​[((∇ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱))​(∇ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱))⊤+∇2ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱))​𝔼ξ​[f​(𝐱;ξ)]],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{x}}\sim\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})}\left[\left(\left(\nabla\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\right)\left(\nabla\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\right)^{\top}+\nabla^{2}\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\right)\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\mathbf{x}};\xi)]\right]\ ,

where (a)(a) comes from the product rule of differentiation, and (b)(b) follows from the fact that ∇π𝜽​(𝐱)=π𝜽​(𝐱)​∇ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱)\nabla\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})=\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})\nabla\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}}). ∎

C.3 Proof of Prop. 3.2

Proof.

Taking the reparametrization trick 𝐱=𝜽+μ​𝐮{\mathbf{x}}={\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}} with 𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}), we have:

∇2Fμ​(𝜽)​=(a)​𝔼𝐮​[(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)​𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)]μ2],\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\overset{(a)}{=}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\left({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}\right)\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)]}{\mu^{2}}\right]\ , (50)

where (a)(a) comes from ∇ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱)=1μ2​(𝐱−𝜽)=1μ​𝐮\nabla\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})=\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}({\mathbf{x}}-{\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{\mu}{\mathbf{u}} and ∇2ln⁡π𝜽​(𝐱)=−1μ2​𝐈d\nabla^{2}\ln\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})=-\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{I}}_{d} for Gaussian policy.

Since 𝔼𝐮​[𝐮𝐮⊤]=𝐈d\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}[{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}]={\mathbf{I}}_{d}, for any constant baseline bb that is independent of 𝐮{\mathbf{u}}, (50) can be further transformed as:

∇2Fμ​(𝜽)=𝔼𝐮​[(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)​𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)]μ2]+b⋅𝔼𝐮​[(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)]=𝔼𝐮​[(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)​𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−b]μ2],\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\left({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}\right)\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)]}{\mu^{2}}\right]+b\cdot\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\left({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}\right)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\left({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}\right)\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-b]}{\mu^{2}}\right]\ , (51)

which completes the proof. ∎

C.4 Proof of Prop. 3.3

Proof.

Regardless of the choice of baseline bb, since 𝔼𝐮​[𝐮𝐮⊤]=𝐈d\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}[{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}]={\mathbf{I}}_{d}, Prop. 3.2 can always be transformed as:

∇2Fμ​(𝜽)=\displaystyle\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})= 𝔼𝐮​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−bμ2​𝐮𝐮⊤]−𝔼𝐮​[𝔼𝐮​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−bμ2]​𝐮𝐮⊤]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-b}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-b}{\mu^{2}}\right]{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}\right] (52)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼𝐮​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−b−𝔼𝐮​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−b]μ2​𝐮𝐮⊤]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-b-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-b\right]}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}\right]
=\displaystyle= 𝔼𝐮​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−𝔼𝐮​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)]μ2​𝐮𝐮⊤],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)\right]}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}\right]\ ,

which completes the proof. ∎

C.5 Proof of Lem. 3.5

Proof.

Suppose there exists another baseline b′≠𝔼𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d)​[𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)]]b^{\prime}\neq\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d})}\left[\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)\right]\right] that also satisfies the unbiasedness:

𝔼𝐮​[𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−b′]μ2​𝐮𝐮⊤]=∇2Fμ​(𝜽)=𝔼𝐮​[𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)]μ2​(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)].\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-b^{\prime}\right]}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}\right]=\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)\right]}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\right]\ . (53)

Take the difference on both sides, we have:

0=\displaystyle 0= 𝔼𝐮​[𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−b′]μ2​𝐮𝐮⊤]−𝔼𝐮​[𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)]μ2​(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-b^{\prime}\right]}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}\right]-\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)\right]}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\right] (54)
=\displaystyle= 𝔼𝐮​[−b′μ2​𝐮𝐮⊤]+𝔼𝐮​[𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)]μ2​𝐈d]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[-\frac{b^{\prime}}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}\right]+\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}\left[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)\right]}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}\right]

Therefore, the average baseline is the unique choice that guarantees the unbiasedness of the Hessian estimator in Prop. 3.3. ∎

C.6 Proof of Prop. 3.7

Proof.

We rewrite the smoothed objective using the importance weight w​(𝐱)=π𝜽​(𝐱)/ρ​(𝐱)w({\mathbf{x}})=\pi_{{\bm{\theta}}}({\mathbf{x}})/\rho({\mathbf{x}}). Proof.

The gradient of the smoothed objective Fμ​(𝜽)F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}) is a direct result of Stein’s identity:

∇Fμ​(𝜽)=𝔼𝐮​[∇F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)]=1μ​𝔼𝐮​[∇𝐮F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)]​=(a)​1μ​𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)​𝐮],\nabla F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\nabla F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})\right]=\frac{1}{\mu}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})\right]\overset{(a)}{=}\frac{1}{\mu}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}){\mathbf{u}}\right]\ , (58)

Then, the Hessian of the smoothed objective Fμ​(𝜽)F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}) can be derived by taking another derivative:

Note that ∇𝐮(F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)​𝐮)=(∇𝐮F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮))​𝐮⊤+F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)​𝐈d\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\quantity(F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}){\mathbf{u}})=\quantity(\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})){\mathbf{u}}^{\top}+F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}){\mathbf{I}}_{d}, we have:

∇2Fμ​(𝜽)=1μ2​𝔼𝐮​[∇𝐮(F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)​𝐮)−F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)​𝐈d]​=(a)​1μ2​𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)​(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)],\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\nabla_{\mathbf{u}}\quantity(F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}){\mathbf{u}})-F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}){\mathbf{I}}_{d}\right]\overset{(a)}{=}\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\right]\ , (60)

where (a)(a) again follows from Stein’s identity. ∎

C.9 Proof of Thm. 4.7

Proof.

Since the baseline bb is a free parameter in the Hessian estimator, to ensure unbiasedness, we consider the Monte Carlo implementation of Prop. 3.2:

𝐇^​(𝜽)=1K​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−bμ2​(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d),\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-b}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\ , (63)

where the baseline bb is a constant independent of the random directions {𝐮k}k=1K\{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}.

We verify that the Hessian estimator in (63) is unbiased:

𝔼​[𝐇^​(𝜽)]​=(a)​𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)−bμ2​(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)]​=(b)​𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)μ2​(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)]​=(c)​∇2Fμ​(𝜽),\mathbb{E}\quantity[\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})]\overset{(a)}{=}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\frac{F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})-b}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\right]\overset{(b)}{=}\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\left[\frac{F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\right]\overset{(c)}{=}\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\ , (64)

where (a)(a) follows from the independence of {𝐮k}\{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\} across different queries kk, (b)(b) uses the property 𝔼𝐮​[𝐮𝐮⊤]=𝐈d\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}]={\mathbf{I}}_{d}, and (c)(c) follows from Stein’s identity.

Next, the variance of the Hessian estimator in (63) is given by:

Var​(𝐇^​(𝜽))=𝔼​[‖𝐇^​(𝜽)−∇2Fμ​(𝜽)‖F2]=𝔼​[‖𝐇^​(𝜽)‖F2]−2​Tr⁡(𝔼​[𝐇^​(𝜽)]⊤​∇2Fμ​(𝜽))+‖∇2Fμ​(𝜽)‖F2\displaystyle\mathrm{Var}\quantity(\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}}))=\mathbb{E}\quantity[\norm{\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})-\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}^{2}]=\mathbb{E}\left[\norm{\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}^{2}\right]-2\Tr\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})\right]^{\top}\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right)+\norm{\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}^{2} (65)
=(a)\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=} 𝔼​[‖1K​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−bμ2​(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d)‖F2]−‖∇2Fμ​(𝜽)‖F2,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\norm{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-b}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})}_{F}^{2}\right]-\norm{\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}^{2}\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from (64).

Differentiating the variance with respect to the baseline bb yields:

∂∂b​Var​(𝐇^​(𝜽))=\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial b}\mathrm{Var}\quantity(\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}}))= 2​𝔼​[⟨1K​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−bμ2​(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d),1K​∑k=1K(−1μ2)​(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d)⟩F]\displaystyle 2\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-b}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}),\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\quantity(-\frac{1}{\mu^{2}})\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\right\rangle_{F}\right] (66)
=(a)\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=} −2K2​μ4​∑k=1K𝔼​[⟨(f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−b)​(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d),(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d)⟩F]\displaystyle-\frac{2}{K^{2}\mu^{4}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left\langle\quantity(f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-b)\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}),\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\right\rangle_{F}\right]
=\displaystyle= −2K2​μ4​∑k=1K𝔼𝐮​[⟨(F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k)−b)​(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d),(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d)⟩F]\displaystyle-\frac{2}{K^{2}\mu^{4}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\left\langle\quantity(F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k})-b)\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}),\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\right\rangle_{F}\right]
=\displaystyle= −2K2​μ4​∑k=1K𝔼𝐮​[(F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k)−b)​‖(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d)‖F2],\displaystyle-\frac{2}{K^{2}\mu^{4}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\left(F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k})-b\right)\norm{\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})}_{F}^{2}\right]\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from the independence of {𝐮k}\{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\} across different queries kk.

b∗=∑k=1K𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k)​‖(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d)‖F2]∑k=1K𝔼𝐮​[‖(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d)‖F2]=𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)​‖(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)‖F2]𝔼𝐮​[‖(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)‖F2].b^{*}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k})\norm{\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})}_{F}^{2}\right]}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\norm{\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})}_{F}^{2}\right]}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})\norm{\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})}_{F}^{2}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\norm{\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})}_{F}^{2}\right]}\ . (67)

In particular, when 𝐮∼𝒩​(0,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(0,{\mathbf{I}}_{d}) as d→∞d\to\infty, such that ‖(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d)‖F2\norm{\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})}_{F}^{2} is effectively constant, the optimal baseline reduces to the expected function value:

b∗=𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)]=Fμ​(𝜽).b^{*}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})\right]=F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\ . (68)

Finally, following the discussion in Appx. D.1, which establishes that Prop. 3.2 with an averaged baseline is equivalent to Def. 4.1, we conclude that the Hessian estimator in Def. 4.1 also attains the minimum variance among all constant baselines. ∎

C.10 Proof of Thm. 4.8

Before proving Thm. 4.8, we first present the variance analysis of the Hessian estimator with the optimal baseline in Thm. 4.7:

Lemma C.7 (Variance of Hessian Estimator).

Consider the Hessian estimator utilizing the optimal baseline derived in Thm. 4.7. Let 𝐮∼𝒩​(𝟎,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},{\mathbf{I}}_{d}). Under Assump. 4.3 and 4.4, the variance of the estimator is bounded by:

𝔼​[‖𝐇^​(𝜽)−∇2Fμ​(𝜽)‖F2]≤K​d​(d+2)​V(K−1)2​μ4,\mathbb{E}\quantity[\norm{\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})-\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}^{2}]\leq\frac{Kd(d+2)V}{(K-1)^{2}\mu^{4}}\ ,

where V≜σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+2)V\triangleq\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+2).

Proof.

We adopt the decomposition of the variance of the Hessian estimator from (65), and let bb be the averaged baseline in Thm. 4.7. Then we have:

≤\displaystyle\leq 𝔼​[‖1K−1​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−bμ2​𝐮k​𝐮k⊤‖F2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\norm{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-b}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}}_{F}^{2}\right]
=(a)\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=} 1(K−1)2​μ4​∑k=1K𝔼​[|f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮k​𝐮k⊤‖F2]\displaystyle\frac{1}{(K-1)^{2}\mu^{4}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}}_{F}^{2}\right]
=\displaystyle= K(K−1)2​μ4​𝔼​[|f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)−Fμ​(𝜽)|2​‖𝐮‖4]\displaystyle\frac{K}{(K-1)^{2}\mu^{4}}\mathbb{E}\left[\left|f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)-F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\right|^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}}^{4}\right]
≤(b)\displaystyle\overset{(b)}{\leq} K​d​(d+2)​V(K−1)2​μ4,\displaystyle\frac{Kd(d+2)V}{(K-1)^{2}\mu^{4}}\ ,

where (a)(a) follows from the independence of {𝐮k}\{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\} across different queries kk, (b)(b) comes from Lem. C.4. Here, we denote V≜σξ2+4​L02​μ2​(d+2)V\triangleq\sigma_{\xi}^{2}+4L_{0}^{2}\mu^{2}(d+2) for simplicity. ∎

Proof.

C.11 Derivation of Def. 5.1

Proof.

The Hessian estimator in Def. 4.1 can be rewritten as:

𝐇^​(𝜽)=1K−1​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−1K​∑k′=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k′;ξ)μ2​𝐮k​𝐮k⊤⋅𝒲​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k)=U​D​U⊤,\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}};\xi)}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}\cdot\mathcal{W}({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k})=UDU^{\top}\ , (71)

where we denote 𝐃=diag⁡(ν1/(K−1),…,νK/(K−1))∈ℝK×K{\mathbf{D}}=\operatorname{diag}(\nu_{1}/\quantity(K-1),\ldots,\nu_{K}/\quantity(K-1))\in{\mathbb{R}}^{K\times K} with νk=f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−1K​∑k′=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k′;ξ)μ2​𝒲​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k)\nu_{k}=\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}};\xi)}{\mu^{2}}\mathcal{W}({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k}), and 𝐔=[𝐮1,𝐮2,…,𝐮K]∈ℝd×K{\mathbf{U}}=[{\mathbf{u}}_{1},{\mathbf{u}}_{2},\ldots,{\mathbf{u}}_{K}]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times K}.

According to the Woodbury matrix identity (Woodbury, 1950), we have:

(𝐇^​(𝜽)+λ​𝐈d)−1=(λ​𝐈d+𝐔𝐃𝐔⊤)−1=1λ​𝐈d−1λ2​𝐔​(𝐃−1+1λ​𝐔⊤​𝐔)−1​𝐔⊤.\quantity(\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})+\lambda{\mathbf{I}}_{d})^{-1}=\quantity(\lambda{\mathbf{I}}_{d}+{\mathbf{U}}{\mathbf{D}}{\mathbf{U}}^{\top})^{-1}=\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}{\mathbf{U}}\quantity({\mathbf{D}}^{-1}+\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{U}}^{\top}{\mathbf{U}})^{-1}{\mathbf{U}}^{\top}\ . (72)

If we consider the diagonal approximation of 𝐔{\mathbf{U}} (i.e. assuming {𝐮k}k=1K\{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} are orthogonal), then 𝐔⊤​𝐔{\mathbf{U}}^{\top}{\mathbf{U}} is a diagonal matrix with the kk-th diagonal element being ‖𝐮k‖2\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2}. The inverse term can be calculated as:

𝐃−1+1λ​𝐔⊤​𝐔=diag⁡(K−1νk+1λ​‖𝐮k‖2)k=1K.{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}+\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{U}}^{\top}{\mathbf{U}}=\operatorname{diag}\quantity(\frac{K-1}{\nu_{k}}+\frac{1}{\lambda}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})_{k=1}^{K}\ . (73)

Therefore, the approximated inverse Hessian 𝐇~−1​(𝜽)\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}}) is:

𝐇~−1​(𝜽)=1λ​𝐈d−1λ2​∑k=1K𝐮k​𝐮k⊤K−1νk+1λ​‖𝐮k‖2=1λ​𝐈d−∑k=1Kνkλ​(λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2)​𝐮k​𝐮k⊤.\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}}{\frac{K-1}{\nu_{k}}+\frac{1}{\lambda}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\nu_{k}}{\lambda\quantity(\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}\ . (74)

C.12 Derivation of Def. 5.3

Proof.

Adopt from inverse Hessian estimator in (15), we have:

𝐇~−1​(𝜽)​∇^​F​(𝜽)=(1λ​𝐈d−∑k=1Kμ​νkλ​(λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2)​𝐮k​𝐮k⊤)​∇^​F.\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}})\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}})=\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\mu\nu_{k}}{\lambda\quantity(\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}\right)\hat{\nabla}F\ . (75)

The first term is simple:

1λ​𝐈d​∇^​F​(𝜽)=1λ​(K−1)​∑k=1Kμ​νk​𝐮k.\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{\lambda(K-1)}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu\nu_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\ . (76)

(∑k=1Kμ​νkλ​(λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2)​𝐮k​𝐮k⊤)​∇^​F​(𝜽)=(∑k=1Kμ​νkλ​(λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2)​𝐮k​𝐮k⊤)​(1K−2​∑k′=1k′≠kKμ​νk′​𝐮k′)\displaystyle\quantity(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\mu\nu_{k}}{\lambda\quantity(\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top})\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}})=\quantity(\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\mu\nu_{k}}{\lambda\quantity(\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top})\quantity(\frac{1}{K-2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k^{\prime}=1\\ k^{\prime}\neq k\end{subarray}}^{K}\mu\nu_{k^{\prime}}{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}}) (77)
=\displaystyle= 1K−2​∑k=1K∑k′=1k′≠kKμ​νk​μ​νk′λ​(λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2)​𝐮k​(𝐮k⊤​𝐮k′)=∑k=1Kμ​νk​𝐮k⊤​(∑k′=1,k′≠kKνk′​𝐮k′)/(K−2)λ​(λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2)​𝐮k.\displaystyle\frac{1}{K-2}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k^{\prime}=1\\ k^{\prime}\neq k\end{subarray}}^{K}\frac{\mu\nu_{k}\mu\nu_{k^{\prime}}}{\lambda\quantity(\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu\nu_{k}\frac{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}\quantity(\sum_{k^{\prime}=1,k^{\prime}\neq k}^{K}\nu_{k^{\prime}}{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}})/\quantity(K-2)}{\lambda\quantity(\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\ .

Combining the two terms together, we have:

𝐇~−1​(𝜽)​∇^​F​(𝜽)=∑k=1Kμ​νk​(1λ​(K−1)−𝐮k⊤​(∑k′=1,k′≠kKνk′​𝐮k′)/(K−2)λ​(λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2))​𝐮k.\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}})\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mu\nu_{k}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda(K-1)}-\frac{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}\quantity(\sum_{k^{\prime}=1,k^{\prime}\neq k}^{K}\nu_{k^{\prime}}{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}})/\quantity(K-2)}{\lambda\quantity(\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})}\right){\mathbf{u}}_{k}\ . (78)

Proof.

We first use Resolvent identity to decompose the error between two inverse Hessians into:

=(a)\displaystyle\overset{(a)}{=} 𝔼​[‖𝐇~−1​(𝜽)​(∇2Fμ​(𝜽)+λ​𝐈d−𝐇~​(𝜽))​(∇2Fμ​(𝜽)+λ​𝐈d)−1‖F2]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\quantity[\norm{\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}})\quantity(\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})+\lambda{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}}))\quantity(\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})+\lambda{\mathbf{I}}_{d})^{-1}}_{F}^{2}]

‖𝐇~−1​(𝜽)‖22=‖1λ​𝐈d−∑k=1Kνkλ​(λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2)​𝐮k​𝐮k⊤‖22.\norm{\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}})}_{2}^{2}=\norm{\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\nu_{k}}{\lambda\quantity(\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}}_{2}^{2}\ . λk=1λ−νk​‖𝐮k‖2λ​(λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2)=K−1λ​(K−1)+νk​‖𝐮k‖2=1λ​(1+tk),\lambda_{k}=\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2}}{\lambda\quantity(\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2})}=\frac{K-1}{\lambda(K-1)+\nu_{k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2}}=\frac{1}{\lambda\quantity(1+t_{k})}\ , (81)

Meanwhile, in the orthogonal complement subspace, the eigenvalues are all 1/λ1/\lambda. Therefore, we have:

C.16 Proof of Thm. B.1

Before proving Thm. B.1, we first present the variance analysis of Hessian estimator with query reuse technique and the optimal baseline in Thm. 4.7:

Consider the Hessian estimator with query reuse in Def. 4.2 utilizing the optimal baseline derived in Thm. 4.7. Let 𝐮∼𝒩​(𝟎,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bm{0},{\mathbf{I}}_{d}). Under Assump. 4.3 and 4.4, the variance of the estimator is bounded by:

Appendix D Additional Discussion

D.1 Equivalence between Prop. 3.2 with Averaged Baseline and Def. 4.1

The Gaussian smoothed Hessian estimator in Prop. 3.2 with the averaged baseline b=𝔼​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)]b=\mathbb{E}\quantity[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)] is given as:

∇2Fμ​(𝜽)=𝔼𝐮​[𝔼ξ​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮;ξ)]−𝔼​[f​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)]μ2​(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d)].\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\left[\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\xi}[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}};\xi)]-\mathbb{E}\quantity[f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)]}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\right]\ . (108)

Moreover, the practical implementation (via Monte Carlo) of the above estimator is:

𝐇^​(𝜽)=1K−1​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−1K​∑k′=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k′;ξ)μ2​(𝐮k​𝐮k⊤−𝐈d),\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}};\xi)}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\ , (109)

where the 1K−1\frac{1}{K-1} factor is used to make the estimator unbiased (similar to Def. 4.1).

The estimator (109) can be further decomposed as:

𝐇^​(𝜽)=\displaystyle\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})= 1K−1​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−1K​∑k′=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k′;ξ)μ2​𝐮k​𝐮k⊤⏟Def. 4.1\displaystyle\underbrace{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}};\xi)}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}{\mathbf{u}}_{k}^{\top}}_{\text{Def.~\ref{def:hess-est}}} (110)
−1K−1​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)−1K​∑k′=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k′;ξ)μ2​𝐈d⏟=0,\displaystyle\quad-\underbrace{\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}};\xi)}{\mu^{2}}{\mathbf{I}}_{d}}_{=0}\ ,

where the first term is exactly the Hessian estimator in Def. 4.1, and the second term equals zero since:

=\displaystyle= (1K−1​∑k=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k;ξ)μ2−KK−1​1K​∑k′=1Kf​(𝜽+μ​𝐮k′;ξ)μ2)​𝐈d\displaystyle\quantity(\frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k};\xi)}{\mu^{2}}-\frac{K}{K-1}\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}\frac{f({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}}_{k^{\prime}};\xi)}{\mu^{2}}){\mathbf{I}}_{d}

D.2 Smoothing Bias vs. Smoothing Radius μ\mu

The Hessian estimator in Thm. 4.6 is unbiased for the Gaussian-smoothed Hessian ∇2Fμ​(𝜽)\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}) rather than the exact Hessian ∇2F​(𝜽)\nabla^{2}F({\bm{\theta}}). The resulting smoothing bias between ∇2Fμ​(𝜽)\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}) and ∇2F​(𝜽)\nabla^{2}F({\bm{\theta}}) is controlled directly by the smoothing radius μ\mu. Below we present the formal bound on the smoothing bias in terms of μ\mu:

Proposition D.1 (Bias of Smoothed Hessian).

Under Assump. 4.3, for 𝐮∼𝒩​(𝟎,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}\sim{\mathcal{N}}({\bm{0}},{\mathbf{I}}_{d}) and Fμ​(𝛉)=𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝛉+μ​𝐮)]F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})=\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})], the Gaussian-smoothed Hessian satisfies:

‖∇2Fμ​(𝜽)−∇2F​(𝜽)‖F≤L2​μ​d.\norm{\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})-\nabla^{2}F({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}\leq L_{2}\mu\sqrt{d}\ . (112)

Remark. Prop. D.1 gives the unsquared version of Lem. C.3, thus the proof is similar. The bound in Prop. D.1 explicitly characterizes the dependence of the smoothing bias on the smoothing radius μ\mu. Thus, decreasing μ\mu reduces the gap between the smoothed and true Hessians linearly. At the same time, the finite-sample variance terms (Thm. 4.8) in these bounds contain inverse powers of μ\mu, so μ\mu should be interpreted as a bias-variance tuning parameter rather than simply set as small as possible in noisy finite-sample estimation.

Empirical Validation.

We also empirically evaluate the Frobenius norm gap ‖∇2Fμ​(𝜽)−∇2F​(𝜽)‖F\norm{\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})-\nabla^{2}F({\bm{\theta}})}_{F} under different smoothing radii on Rosenbrock and Styblinski-Tang functions to validate Prop. D.1.

As shown in Fig. 4, the bias (Frobenius norm gap) proportionally increases with μ\mu in a log-log scale, with slopes approximately around 11, matching the linear dependence predicted by Prop. D.1. These results indicate that the smoothing bias is well controlled for sufficiently small μ\mu.

D.3 Connection Between Optimal Baseline and Control Variates

The optimal baseline result in Thm. 4.7 can be interpreted as a direct analogue of the classical control variate principle (Asmussen and Glynn, 2007). For the Gaussian Hessian identity in Prop. 3.2, define the random matrix variables:

𝐀​(𝐮)≜F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)μ2​(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d),𝐁​(𝐮)≜1μ2​(𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d).{\mathbf{A}}({\mathbf{u}})\triangleq\frac{F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}),\qquad{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}})\triangleq\frac{1}{\mu^{2}}\quantity({\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d})\ . (113)

Since 𝔼𝐮​[𝐁​(𝐮)]=𝟎\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}[{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}})]={\bm{0}}, the baseline estimator can be written as 𝐀​(𝐮)−b​𝐁​(𝐮){\mathbf{A}}({\mathbf{u}})-b{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}}) and remains unbiased for any constant bb that is independent of 𝐮{\mathbf{u}}:

𝔼𝐮​[𝐀​(𝐮)−b​𝐁​(𝐮)]=𝔼𝐮​[𝐀​(𝐮)]=∇2Fμ​(𝜽).\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}[{\mathbf{A}}({\mathbf{u}})-b{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}})]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}[{\mathbf{A}}({\mathbf{u}})]=\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})\ . (114)

Thus, the baseline term is a zero-mean control variate whose coefficient is chosen only to reduce variance, not to change the target expectation.

Because the estimator is matrix-valued, the natural scalar criterion is the Frobenius variance,

minb∈ℝ⁡𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐀​(𝐮)−b​𝐁​(𝐮)−∇2Fμ​(𝜽)‖F2].\min_{b\in{\mathbb{R}}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\quantity[\norm{{\mathbf{A}}({\mathbf{u}})-b{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}})-\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}^{2}]\ . (115)

Differentiating with respect to bb gives

b∗=𝔼𝐮​[⟨𝐀​(𝐮)−∇2Fμ​(𝜽),𝐁​(𝐮)⟩F]𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐁​(𝐮)‖F2]=𝔼𝐮​[⟨𝐀​(𝐮),𝐁​(𝐮)⟩F]𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐁​(𝐮)‖F2]=𝔼𝐮​[F​(𝜽+μ​𝐮)​‖𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d‖F2]𝔼𝐮​[‖𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d‖F2],b^{*}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\quantity[\left\langle{\mathbf{A}}({\mathbf{u}})-\nabla^{2}F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}),{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}})\right\rangle_{F}]}{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\quantity[\norm{{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}})}_{F}^{2}]}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\quantity[\left\langle{\mathbf{A}}({\mathbf{u}}),{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}})\right\rangle_{F}]}{\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}\quantity[\norm{{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}})}_{F}^{2}]}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\quantity[F({\bm{\theta}}+\mu{\mathbf{u}})\norm{{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}}_{F}^{2}]}{\mathbb{E}_{{\mathbf{u}}}\quantity[\norm{{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}}_{F}^{2}]}\ , (116)

where the second equality uses 𝔼𝐮​[𝐁​(𝐮)]=𝟎\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{u}}[{\mathbf{B}}({\mathbf{u}})]={\bm{0}}. This is exactly the optimal baseline in (13). When ‖𝐮𝐮⊤−𝐈d‖F2\norm{{\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\top}-{\mathbf{I}}_{d}}_{F}^{2} concentrates in high dimensions, the coefficient reduces to Fμ​(𝜽)F_{\mu}({\bm{\theta}}), which is estimated in practice by the averaged baseline.

D.4 Exact Woodbury Inverse vs. Approximate Inverse Hessian

The inverse Hessian approximation in Def. 5.1 replaces the full Gram matrix 𝐔⊤​𝐔{\mathbf{U}}^{\top}{\mathbf{U}} in the exact Woodbury inverse with its diagonal part. This step is exact when the random directions are pairwise orthogonal. For Gaussian directions, it is also accurate in high dimensions because the diagonal terms ‖𝐮k‖2\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}}^{2} are of order dd, while the off-diagonal terms 𝐮i⊤​𝐮j{\mathbf{u}}_{i}^{\top}{\mathbf{u}}_{j} are only of order d\sqrt{d} for i≠ji\neq j. The following proposition gives the resulting approximation error.

Proposition D.2 (Exact and Approximate Inverse Error).

Let 𝐔=[𝐮1,…,𝐮K]∈ℝd×K{\mathbf{U}}=[{\mathbf{u}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{u}}_{K}]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d\times K} with 𝐮k∼i.i.d.𝒩​(𝟎,𝐈d){\mathbf{u}}_{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mathrm{i.i.d.}}}{{\sim}}{\mathcal{N}}({\bm{0}},{\mathbf{I}}_{d}). Define 𝐆≜𝐔⊤​𝐔{\mathbf{G}}\triangleq{\mathbf{U}}^{\top}{\mathbf{U}}, Δ≜diag⁡(𝐆)\Delta\triangleq\operatorname{diag}({\mathbf{G}}), and 𝐄≜𝐆−Δ{\mathbf{E}}\triangleq{\mathbf{G}}-\Delta. Let

𝐌≜𝐃−1+1λ​𝐆,𝐌~≜𝐃−1+1λ​Δ,{\mathbf{M}}\triangleq{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}+\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{G}},\quad\widetilde{{\mathbf{M}}}\triangleq{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}+\frac{1}{\lambda}\Delta\ , (117)

where 𝐃{\mathbf{D}} is defined as in Def. 5.1. Assume λ>0\lambda>0 is fixed, ‖𝐃−1‖2=𝒪p​(1)\norm{{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}}_{2}=\mathcal{O}_{p}(1). Then,

‖(𝐇^​(𝜽)+λ​𝐈d)−1−𝐇~−1​(𝜽)‖F=𝒪p​(Kd).\norm{\quantity(\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})+\lambda{\mathbf{I}}_{d})^{-1}-\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}=\mathcal{O}_{p}\quantity(\frac{K}{\sqrt{d}})\ . (118)
Proof.

From (14) and (15), the only difference between the exact inverse and the approximation is whether 𝐌−1{\mathbf{M}}^{-1} or 𝐌~−1\widetilde{{\mathbf{M}}}^{-1} is used in the low-dimensional Woodbury correction:

(𝐇^​(𝜽)+λ​𝐈d)−1−𝐇~−1​(𝜽)=−1λ2​𝐔​(𝐌−1−𝐌~−1)​𝐔⊤.\quantity(\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})+\lambda{\mathbf{I}}_{d})^{-1}-\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}})=-\frac{1}{\lambda^{2}}{\mathbf{U}}\quantity({\mathbf{M}}^{-1}-\widetilde{{\mathbf{M}}}^{-1}){\mathbf{U}}^{\top}\ . (119)

For Gaussian directions, standard concentration gives ‖𝐔‖22=‖𝐆‖2=𝒪p​(d)\norm{{\mathbf{U}}}_{2}^{2}=\norm{{\mathbf{G}}}_{2}=\mathcal{O}_{p}(d), ‖Δ‖2=Θp​(d)\norm{\Delta}_{2}=\Theta_{p}(d), and ‖𝐄‖F=𝒪p​(K​d)\norm{{\mathbf{E}}}_{F}=\mathcal{O}_{p}(K\sqrt{d}), since the off-diagonal entries 𝐮i⊤​𝐮j{\mathbf{u}}_{i}^{\top}{\mathbf{u}}_{j} have variance dd for i≠ji\neq j. Because ‖𝐃−1‖2=𝒪p​(1)\norm{{\mathbf{D}}^{-1}}_{2}=\mathcal{O}_{p}(1) and λ\lambda is fixed, the diagonal matrix 𝐌~\widetilde{{\mathbf{M}}} has entries of order dd, hence ‖𝐌~−1‖2=𝒪p​(d−1)\norm{\widetilde{{\mathbf{M}}}^{-1}}_{2}=\mathcal{O}_{p}(d^{-1}).

By the assumed stability of the exact Woodbury inverse, ‖𝐌−1‖2=𝒪p​(d−1)\norm{{\mathbf{M}}^{-1}}_{2}=\mathcal{O}_{p}(d^{-1}). Then, by the resolvent identity,

𝐌−1−𝐌~−1=−1λ​𝐌−1​𝐄​𝐌~−1.{\mathbf{M}}^{-1}-\widetilde{{\mathbf{M}}}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{\lambda}{\mathbf{M}}^{-1}{\mathbf{E}}\widetilde{{\mathbf{M}}}^{-1}. (120)

Therefore,

‖(𝐇^​(𝜽)+λ​𝐈d)−1−𝐇~−1​(𝜽)‖F≤1λ3​‖𝐔‖22​‖𝐌−1‖2​‖𝐄‖F​‖𝐌~−1‖2\displaystyle\norm{\quantity(\widehat{{\mathbf{H}}}({\bm{\theta}})+\lambda{\mathbf{I}}_{d})^{-1}-\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}})}_{F}\leq\frac{1}{\lambda^{3}}\norm{{\mathbf{U}}}_{2}^{2}\norm{{\mathbf{M}}^{-1}}_{2}\norm{{\mathbf{E}}}_{F}\norm{\widetilde{{\mathbf{M}}}^{-1}}_{2} (121)
=\displaystyle= 𝒪p​(d)⋅𝒪p​(d−1)⋅𝒪p​(K​d)⋅𝒪p​(d−1)=𝒪p​(Kd),\displaystyle\ \mathcal{O}_{p}(d)\cdot\mathcal{O}_{p}(d^{-1})\cdot\mathcal{O}_{p}(K\sqrt{d})\cdot\mathcal{O}_{p}(d^{-1})=\mathcal{O}_{p}\quantity(\frac{K}{\sqrt{d}})\ ,

which completes the proof. ∎

Remark. Prop. D.2 formalizes the intuition behind the diagonal Gram approximation in (15). The result keeps the dependence on the number of query directions as 𝒪p​(K/d)\mathcal{O}_{p}(K/\sqrt{d}). For the small fixed KK used in our experiments, this reduces to the d−1/2d^{-1/2} decay observed empirically. Thus, the approximation becomes increasingly accurate in the high-dimensional regimes targeted by ZoVH, while avoiding the need to manipulate dense d×dd\times d inverse matrices.

Empirical Validation.

We further empirically measure the Frobenius norm error between the exact Woodbury inverse in (14) and the approximation in (15).

As shown in Fig. 5, the error decreases consistently as the dimension increases. The fitted slopes are close to −0.5-0.5 across four synthetic functions, matching the d−1/2d^{-1/2} dependence in Prop. D.2. The result supports using the approximate inverse for the small KK setting used by ZoVH, especially in LLM fine-tuning where individual layers contain millions of parameters.

D.5 Inverse Hessian-Gradient Product Approximation with Query Reuse

Definition D.3 (Shared Product with Query Reuse).

Assume 𝐇~−1​(𝜽)\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}}) and ∇^​F​(𝜽)\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}) are estimated using the same set of standard Gaussian directions {𝐮k}k=1K\{{\mathbf{u}}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}. The bias-corrected inverse Hessian-gradient product 𝐇~−1​(𝜽)​∇^​F​(𝜽)\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}})\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}) with query reuse is given by:

𝐇~−1​(𝜽t−1)​∇^​F​(𝜽t−1)≜∑i,k=1N,Kμ​νt−i,kλ​(1N​K−1−𝐮t−i,k⊤​(∑(j,k′)≠(i,k)νt−j,k′​𝐮t−j,k′)/(N​K−2)λ​(N​K−1)+νt−i,k​‖𝐮t−i,k‖2)​𝐮t−i,k.\widetilde{{\mathbf{H}}}^{-1}({\bm{\theta}}_{t-1})\hat{\nabla}F({\bm{\theta}}_{t-1})\triangleq\sum_{i,k=1}^{N,K}\frac{\mu\nu_{t-i,k}}{\lambda}\quantity(\frac{1}{NK-1}-\frac{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-i,k}^{\top}\left(\sum\limits_{(j,k^{\prime})\neq(i,k)}\nu_{t-j,k^{\prime}}{\mathbf{u}}_{t-j,k^{\prime}}\right)/(NK-2)}{\lambda(NK-1)+\nu_{t-i,k}\norm{{\mathbf{u}}_{t-i,k}}^{2}}){\mathbf{u}}_{t-i,k}. (122)

where the averaged baseline b^t≜1N​K​∑i,k=1N,Kyt−i,k\hat{b}_{t}\triangleq\frac{1}{NK}\sum_{i,k=1}^{N,K}y_{t-i,k}, and νt−i,k≜(yt−i,k−b^t)/μ2\nu_{t-i,k}\triangleq\quantity(y_{t-i,k}-\hat{b}_{t})/\mu^{2}.

Remark. The definition above extends Def. 5.3 to incorporate query reuse across NN iterations. By reusing the same set of KK random directions over NN consecutive iterations, we effectively increase the sample size to N​KNK, which enhances the accuracy of both the Hessian and gradient estimations. This approach leverages historical query information, reducing the need for additional function evaluations while maintaining robust optimization performance.

D.6 Comparison with HiZOO (Zhao et al., 2025)

HiZOO (Zhao et al., 2025) is a recently proposed curvature-aware zeroth-order optimization method that utilizes a randomized central-difference Hessian estimator (5) for memory-efficient LLMs fine-tuning. However, to avoid the computational complexity of inverting the full Hessian estimator, HiZOO only approximates the diagonal of the Hessian estimator to facilitate inversion. Besides, recent studies (Zhang et al., 2024) have shown that the practical Hessian of LLMs exhibits significant block-diagonal structures, indicating that simple diagonal approximations may overlook important curvature information.

In contrast, our proposed method ZoVH addresses this by approximating the full Hessian matrix and captures more comprehensive curvature information than diagonal approximations. This leads to more accurate inverse Hessian-gradient products, which are crucial for effective optimization steps. A detailed comparison of HiZOO and ZoVH in terms of Hessian approximation and its inverse is summarized in Table 2.

Appendix E Additional Experiments

E.1 Curvature-Aware Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-Tuning

Recent advancements in memory-efficient fine-tuning for large language models (LLMs) have begun to leverage zeroth-order optimization (Malladi et al., 2023) and curvature-aware techniques (Zhao et al., 2025). However, conventional ZO Hessian approximations often suffer from high variance, which can hamper convergence during fine-tuning. ZoVH addresses this limitation by reducing variance through a provably averaged baseline and the reuse of historical query information. In this section, we apply ZoVH to curvature-aware ZO fine-tuning of LLMs, comparing its performance against MeZO (Malladi et al., 2023) and HiZOO (Zhao et al., 2025) (detailed in Appx. F.4). Specifically, we fine-tune OPT-1.3B and OPT-13B (Zhang et al., 2022) on five downstream tasks from the GLUE (Wang et al., 2018) and SuperGLUE (Wang et al., 2020) benchmarks, including SST2, COPA, SQuAD, WSC, and WIC.

Results.

As shown in Fig. 6, ZoVH exhibits faster convergence than both MeZO and HiZOO across distinct tasks and model sizes. Furthermore, ZoVH with N=2N=2 (incorporating query reuse) accelerates convergence further while achieving test accuracy comparable to, or even exceeding, that of ZoVH with N=1N=1 (without query reuse). The test accuracy for all methods is summarized in Tab. 3. ZoVH secures the highest accuracy on the majority of tasks, as well as the highest average accuracy across both models. Notably, ZoVH with N=2N=2 results in lower accuracy on certain tasks compared to N=1N=1. This reflects the bias-variance tradeoff inherent in query reuse, where bias may eventually dominate the total error near convergence. In practice, this issue can be alleviated by reducing the reuse parameter NN as the optimization approaches convergence.

It is worth noting that HiZOO demonstrates inferior performance compared to MeZO in both convergence speed and test accuracy. This underperformance is likely due to the Hessian smoothing factor α\alpha in HiZOO, which is set to a small value (e.g., α=10−8\alpha=10^{-8}, refer to Appx. F.4) to guarantee numerical stability when inverting the diagonal Hessian estimator (while higher α\alpha values leads to divergence issues in our experiments). Consequently, such a small α\alpha may provide negligible regularization, leading to behavior that is practically indistinguishable from MeZO. Additionally, HiZOO requires 33 function queries per step, whereas MeZO uses only 22. Since we evaluate performance under a fixed query budget (as shown in Fig. 6 and Tab. 3), HiZOO completes fewer optimization steps, further contributing to its degraded performance.

Runtime and Memory Overhead.

We also measure wall-clock running time and peak GPU memory on the OPT-13B fine-tuning experiments to evaluate the practical overhead of the inverse Hessian-gradient product in Def. D.3. Tab. 4 reports the results.

As shown in Tab. 4, ZoVH is close to HiZOO in both running time and peak memory usage, while being only slightly slower than MeZO. Compared with HiZOO, ZoVH increases running time by about 5%5\% and peak memory by only 0.040.04 GB. The wall-clock overhead remains small because forward evaluations dominate the runtime, and the additional inverse-Hessian computation only uses scalar coefficients and random directions reconstructed from their seeds. The memory overhead is also limited, since the history buffer stores only N​KNK scalar function values and their corresponding random seeds, rather than the full perturbation vectors. Its persistent memory cost is therefore 𝒪​(N​K)\mathcal{O}(NK) and does not grow with the model dimension.

E.2 Ablation Study for Averaged Baseline and Query Reuse

We further isolate the individual contributions of the averaged baseline and query reuse in ZoVH. The ablation is conducted on four synthetic optimization benchmarks with d=5000d=5000. We compare four variants that differ only in the baseline choice and whether query reuse is enabled. The anchor baseline variants use b=F​(𝜽)b=F({\bm{\theta}}), while the averaged baseline variants use (8). The query reuse variants use the same history setting as the synthetic optimization experiments with N=4N=4.

As shown in Fig. 7, most of the gain comes from replacing the anchor baseline with the averaged baseline, regardless of whether query reuse is used. The averaged baseline curves descend much faster and reach substantially lower optimality gaps than their anchor baseline counterparts. This supports the variance-minimization role of the averaged baseline established in Thm. 4.7. Query reuse provides an additional gain by enlarging the effective sample size without adding new function evaluations, especially in the early and middle stages of optimization. The best performance is achieved when the averaged baseline and query reuse are combined. This is consistent with the bias-variance discussion in Thm. B.1, where a moderate history length reduces variance while the iterate drift remains small enough that the additional reuse bias does not dominate.

Appendix F Experiments Setup

F.1 Empirical Error Analysis of Hessian Approximation

Baselines.

The compared estimators include the two-point (3), three-point (4) Stein Estimators, the randomized central-difference estimator (5), and our proposed ZoVH w/ and w/o the query reuse technique. The one-point Stein estimator (2) is excluded from the comparison due to its significantly higher error than other methods.

Synthetic Functions.

All experiments are conducted in d=5000d=5000 dimensions, and averaged over 500500 test points Hessian errors (2020 random initializations with 2525 test points collected along the optimization trajectory). The analytical forms of the synthetic functions used in our experiments are as follows:

  • •

    Quadratic Function:

    F​(𝜽)=12​𝜽T​𝐀​𝜽+𝒃T​𝜽+c,F({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{2}{\bm{\theta}}^{T}{\mathbf{A}}{\bm{\theta}}+{\bm{b}}^{T}{\bm{\theta}}+c\ , (123)

    where 𝐀{\mathbf{A}} is a symmetric positive-definite matrix, bb is a dd-dimensional vector, and cc is a scalar constant.

  • •

    Rosenbrock Function:

    F​(𝜽)=∑i=1d−1[100​(θi+1−θi2)2+(1−θi)2].F({\bm{\theta}})=\sum_{i=1}^{d-1}\left[100(\theta_{i+1}-\theta_{i}^{2})^{2}+(1-\theta_{i})^{2}\right]\ . (124)
  • •

    Styblinski-Tang Function:

    F​(𝜽)=12​∑i=1d(θi4−16​θi2+50​θi).F({\bm{\theta}})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\left(\theta_{i}^{4}-16\theta_{i}^{2}+50\theta_{i}\right)\ . (125)

Neural Network Hessian.

We further evaluate the Hessian approximation error on a small convolutional neural network (CNN), which consists of two convolutional layers, followed by two fully connected layers. In Fig. 3, we present the empirical Hessian approximation errors across the first convolutional layer (d=96d=96), the second convolutional layer (d=6144d=6144), and the second fully connected layer (d=1280d=1280). This model is trained on the MNIST dataset (LeCun et al., 1998) for digit classification. All experiments are averaged over 56255625 test points Hessian errors (33 independent runs with 18751875 test points collected along each optimization trajectory).

F.2 Synthetic Function Optimization

Baselines.

We compare ZoVH with several representative ZO optimization methods as baselines:

  • •

    Vanilla ZOO (Nesterov and Spokoiny, 2017). This is the standard stochastic finite-difference gradient estimation, whose analytical form is similar to (6), except the averaged baseline bb replaced with anchor baseline b=f​(𝜽;ξ)b=f({\bm{\theta}};\xi).

  • •

    HiZOO (Zhao et al., 2025). This is a recent curvature-aware ZO optimization method that utilizes a randomized central-difference Hessian estimator (5) with diagonal approximation for LLMs fine-tuning. The complete comparison between HiZOO and ZoVH is detailed in Appx. D.6. We do not include ZOHA (Ye et al., 2025) as a separate baseline because HiZOO already covers this case. When the scaling factor is set to 11, HiZOO reduces to ZOHA.

  • •

    ZoAR (Qiu et al., 2025). This is a variance-reduced ZO optimization method that incorporates averaged baseline and query reuse techniques to improve gradient estimation.

F.3 Black-Box Adversarial Attack

Baselines.

The compared methods are the same as in the synthetic experiments in Sec. F.2.

Hyperparameter Settings.

For the black-box adversarial attack, we use the same model as in (Shu et al., 2025): a simple two-layer CNN trained on the MNIST dataset. All experiments are averaged over 1010 independent runs. To ensure fair comparison, all hyperparameters are chosen to achieve the best performance of each method (summarized in Tab. 6).

F.4 Curvature-Aware Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-tuning

Baselines.

We compare ZoVH with two representative ZO optimization methods as baselines:

  • •

    MeZO (Malladi et al., 2023). A memory-efficient ZO fine-tuning method for LLMs that employs a central-difference gradient estimator.

  • •

    HiZOO (Zhao et al., 2025). A recent curvature-aware ZO optimization method that leverages a randomized central-difference Hessian estimator (5) with a diagonal approximation for LLM fine-tuning. A comprehensive comparison between HiZOO and ZoVH is provided in Appx. D.6. We do not include ZOHA (Ye et al., 2025) as a separate baseline because HiZOO already covers this case. When the scaling factor is set to 11, HiZOO reduces to ZOHA.

Hyperparameter Settings.

All experiments are averaged over 33 independent runs. To ensure fair comparison, all hyperparameters are chosen to achieve the best performance of each method (summarized in Tab. 7).
